content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird; the thigh meat is rich in protein, iron and zinc. When cooked with the skin, fats are retained, giving the dish juiciness and a deep flavor. This cut is commonly used in soups, stews and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thigh meat contains more fat than breast, making it more tender after cooking.
Turkey skin is high in collagen, which turns into gelatin during long simmering, enriching broth texture.
In the United States turkey is traditionally served at Thanksgiving, but thighs are a staple in everyday meals.
Turkey meat has a lighter color than chicken due to a higher myoglobin content.
Culinary recipes often marinate turkey in spices and acid (lemon, vinegar) to boost flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Turkey thigh provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are essential for immune function, DNA synthesis and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6 and B12 help protein metabolism and maintain nervous system health.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: When simmered, the skin releases gelatin, which may benefit joint and skin health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Turkey is suitable for low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugars.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Thigh with skin has higher saturated fat, so people with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella and Campylobacter.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Sodium in prepared dishes
items.content: If the thigh is cooked in pre‑made sauces, the salt level can be high.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the thigh in broth, then slice and add to salads, soups, or use as a filling for pies. The skin can be left on for extra flavor or removed after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portioned bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before serving.
